blocks.text: The fall of Jehoiachin was not Judah's final destruction. Babylon's imperial policy involved reducing the kingdom in stages: first, in 597 BCE, Jehoiachin and selected groups of royal, military, administrative, and skilled personnel were removed from Jerusalem; later, when Zedekiah revolted, Jerusalem itself was destroyed and additional deportations occurred in 587/586 BCE. This staged process, preserved in both Kings and Jeremiah, prevents readers from treating the Babylonian exile as a single undifferentiated event.

Palace ration lists recovered from Nebuchadnezzar's reign provide archaeological evidence that Jehoiachin, identified as king of Judah, continued to receive maintenance and food allocations in Babylon along with his dependents and other Judeans. These tablets confirm his official recognition in the Babylonian court after deportation, though they do not address the circumstances of his later release recorded in 2 Kings 25.
